title: A visual archive of the effects of climate change in South Asia - Frontline Magazine
full_text:
Over the past decade, I have been building a visual archive capturing the immediate aftermath of environmental disruptions across India and South Asia. It began in 2013 as a product of humanitarian fieldwork and then evolved into something more reflective: a sustained enquiry into what it means to live through recurring climate events. The archive now stands as a testament to both loss and survival, as the selection of images here proves.
In recent decades, natural disasters have ceased to feel exceptional. Floods return before the previous year’s silt has settled. Heat lingers far beyond its welcome. Rains arrive with unfamiliar force. What was once described as a “once in a century” event recurs within a single decade. In this repetition, something has subtly shifted, not only in the landscapes but also in the psyche of those inhabiting them. Communities now rebuild their lives not with continuation in mind but with the pragmatism of knowing that everything might be gone again, very soon. In such a scenario, architecture becomes provisional, memory shortens, and disaster preparedness becomes instinctive.
The images were often made within hours or days of impact, with the waterlines still visible on trees, the soil still unstable underfoot, and livelihoods in disarray. As such, they are suspended in the shifting space between loss and adaptation. Taken across river basins, coastal belts, agrarian settlements, and temporary shelters, the photographs observe families in altered terrains as they tend to what remains: livestock, children, threatened health, fragments of home. Groups gather in an uncertain pause, children watch without fully understanding, elders stare not with shock or surprise but with recognition.
The climate discourse is often expressed through graphs, projections, or images of aerial devastation. In contrast, this series insists on proximity. It looks at faces, hands, texture of the earth after saturation, displaced livestock. The human body becomes the unit of measurement, both of loss and adaptation.
Over time, the archive has revealed patterns beyond immediate crises: of environmental disruption intersecting with the existing fault lines of poverty, caste, land rights, or of fragile infrastructure. The vulnerable absorb the first and the worst impact. But they are also the architects of adaptation. They innovate quietly, salvaging materials, sharing shelter, adjusting migration routes, and reorganising domestic spaces around new risks. Families from villages, urban, and peri-urban areas often occupy the same frame here, suggesting that the burden of climate disasters is rarely borne alone. The archive asks, what does resilience look like when it is not heroic but habitual?
It also raises vital questions about ways of seeing: how does a photographer maintain ethical clarity in the face of disaster? How to make sameness resonate with the audience? How to photograph adaptation without suggesting acceptance? I will consider the project successful if these images make you see climate change not as spectacle but as an everyday occurrence, re-evaluated in human terms.
Siddharth Behl is a documentary photojournalist and a National Geographic explorer based out of New Delhi. His works are chiefly social documentaries focussed on climate change, migration, refugees, and historical research.

title: Utilising Urban Planning to Address Climate Change as a Health Crisis - orfonline.org
full_text:
Shriya Malhotra, “Utilising Urban Planning to Address Climate Change as a Health Crisis,” ORF Issue Brief No. 891, Observer Research Foundation, July 2026.
The direct link between the climate crisis and human as well as ecological health is widely acknowledged by institutions such as the World Health Organization (WHO)[1] and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC),[2] which formalised their alignment on the subject during the UN Climate Change Conference (COP28) in 2023. The IPCC Assessment Report 6 of the same year concluded that climate change is a “threat to human wellbeing and planetary health,” and that delayed actions will close “the rapidly narrowing window” to secure a liveable future. Climate change is already causing adverse impacts on human health through heat stress, food and water insecurity, infectious diseases, and mental health burdens.[3]
The greenhouse effect and rising temperatures in urban spaces are linked to numerous health issues: increased deaths from dehydration and heat strokes, illnesses due to epidemic outbreaks, kidney stresses due to chronic dehydration, and assorted cardiovascular issues due to chronic heat exposure.[4] Environmental toxicity from unregulated transport and construction emissions, waste/effluents from assorted industries, and poor solid waste management has resulted in water-borne pollutants that could have serious population and environmental health consequences. These are partially the result of unplanned, vehicle-oriented urbanisation across the country, prioritising tourism infrastructure, and focusing on gross domestic product (GDP) rather than ecological well-being and human development.
To be sure, the climate crisis is not experienced equally, and within the Global South, cities are at higher risk of disaster vulnerability due to continued excessive construction, transport-related emissions, and growing population density. WHO maintains, “Climate change, pandemics and rising inequalities remain a threat and underscore the urgency for building resilient health systems.”[5] Much remains to be done to tackle the ever-growing burden of communicable and non-communicable diseases.[6]
Between 1995-2004, extreme weather events such as intense heatwaves and storms accounted for 66 percent of the global climate impact, with the Global South bearing disproportionate losses due to its many vulnerabilities.[7] The losses beyond labour productivity are less quantifiable. Ninety percent of urban population growth is projected to be in Asia and Africa,[8] increasing the exposure of vulnerable communities that already lack climate resilience. This is despite countries of the Global South historically contributing lower emissions per capita.
The impact is gravest on those who lack the agency to participate in planning or economic processes: children, migrants, refugees, the poor, and other vulnerable groups. Infants and the elderly have been exposed to 7.7 and 8.4 heatwave days per year, respectively.[9] Unprecedented heatwaves in 2023 (following the global breach of the 1.5 °C threshold) exposed people to unbearable heat stress as well as more frequent, extreme, and recurring weather-related disasters.[10]
Studies by WHO[11] and IPCC[12] indicate that the impact of climate change in India is worse than in other countries.[13] Indeed, Indian cities epitomise the Global South's climate-health nexus, where dense populations collide with unplanned growth, amplifying threats like heatwaves, floods, droughts, and pollution. In mega-cities including Delhi and Mumbai, levels of emissions measured as AQI (Air Quality Index), specifically of PM2.5, far exceed WHO standards. According to The Lancet, air pollution from burning coal, as well as oil and gas, has resulted in the deaths of an estimated 1.7 million Indians in 2022, an estimated 38-percent increase since 2010;[14] fossil fuels alone are responsible for some 750,000 of those deaths. WHO projects 250,000 additional global deaths yearly from 2030–2050 due to climate-attributable malnutrition, malaria, diarrhoea, and heat stress. The urban heat island (UHI) effect—where concrete can raise temperatures 5-12°C above rural baselines and trap heat overnight, preventing recovery—is seen in the 20-30 percent increase in hospital admissions during peak temperature periods.[15] The loss of tree cover further compounds the effect of heat traps in cities.[16]
The health impacts of climate change in Indian cities are the interconnected consequences of unplanned urbanisation, the loss of natural systems, and inadequate community-based planning and preparedness. A single planning failure, such as unregulated construction in a floodplain, can generate interrelated and recurring health crises. For example, destroyed drains are prone to waterlogging that breeds disease vectors; construction dust and debris worsen air quality and cause respiratory illnesses; the loss of green cover removes carbon traps and intensifies UHI; and forced displacement (even temporary) generates psychosocial stress and mental health burdens. These impacts compound each other in ways that thematic policy silos cannot capture. Thus, understanding the socio-political and ecological networks as an integrated system requiring a multifaceted approach is essential for effective disaster management. Supporting assorted networks for disaster response and preparedness across demographics is especially important, as is leveraging arts and culture to make it context-specific.
Devising an integrated systems framework means demonstrating how human and environmental health impacts are not disparate problems but are interconnected consequences of the same planning failures. Instead of identifying separate health impacts, it contextualises how a planning decision affects assorted health outcomes that tend to compound each other.
Inequalities and poverty in cities of the Global South have accentuated these populations’ vulnerability. The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) reports: “As the impacts of climate change escalate, they can perpetuate or even aggravate cycles of inequality, deepening health and social inequities within and between countries. Marginalised communities, who are least equipped to cope with the effects, often bear the brunt of these impacts.”
India’s urban governance has systemically prioritised GDP-linked infrastructure over climate-adaptive land use.[17] The pursuit of growth and profit maximisation has led to the overexploitation of resources, excessive greenhouse gas emissions, and wide-ranging environmental degradation. Development norms increasingly view the environment as a resource; tourism and GDP-led development have therefore displaced human well-being indicators like health in the hierarchy of priorities. As a result, environmental and human well-being are now at the mercy of competitive market and consumption patterns, compounded by fiscally poor and unaccountable governance.
Highways, high-rises, and parking infrastructure, once built, are very expensive to retrofit for climate resilience.[18] Yet, urban planning is often leveraged to accommodate private vehicles rather than people. A significant share of urban development in India has occurred informally, outside of the purview of master plans, creating a built environment that is structurally resistant to climate adaptation. Heat-trapping materials like metal, glass, and concrete are predominant. Pedestrians tend to experience them at pavements, benches, bus stops, and other smaller infrastructure. A lack of thoughtful design and the use of inappropriate, heat-trapping materials create a heat lock-in effect, which only tends to worsen with time.
Bahadur and Tanner and other scholars[19] highlight a lack of targeted financing mechanisms;[20] fractured responsibilities across municipal bodies and state agencies mean that no single entity is accountable for climate health impact. The shortage of urban planners and regulatory frameworks results in land use zoning that ignores informal settlements or the health of natural resources. Top-down approaches also tend to bypass local governments while prioritising national benchmarks over city-specific issues. Limited public participation and rigid hierarchies present easy adaptability, while the views and experiences of vulnerable groups are often omitted in mainstream planning. As one analyst observes, “Urban India’s future will depend on bridging the chasm between legal provisions and lived realities, a process demanding bold, participatory reform.”[21]
Urban planning as an interdisciplinary field offers a way to direct and design resilience for land, infrastructure, and services as they become increasingly urban. Planners use diverse disciplines for policy, such as land use, transport, and housing that may benefit health. In the context of disaster risk reduction (DRR), they may also be used to democratise public spaces and strengthen networks for preparedness through creative scenario building.
The question of how to involve communities and other groups, particularly those that are more vulnerable in climate and health action and preparedness, becomes more pertinent during discussions about leveraging urban planning as an intervention. The work of Mariana Mazzicato[22] suggests leveraging the role of arts and culture as integral to processes like development and infrastructure. Governments may also leverage experts and specialists (including, for instance, conservationists rather than contractors). This section examines three specific mechanisms through which grassroots urban planning can address the climate-health nexus in Indian cities.
Art can play an important and engaging role in explaining climate science (including health risks), which requires as much communication and organising support as possible and cannot be left up to either government or businesses. Tapping into the ideas, knowledge, and insights of those who understand context is crucial for future resilience and effective responses to climate change: for instance, vernacular forms of architecture are an effective path towards climate-resilient construction.
Creative problem-solving can help strengthen cities’ responses to climate disruption, particularly when deployed through grassroots and community-led initiatives. Public art, participatory urban design, and other site-specific visual communication can communicate abstract climate risks—such as heat stress, flooding, air pollution, and water scarcity—into lived, relatable information that informs behaviour and builds collective preparedness. Community murals, street theatre, wayfinding design, and co-created public spaces can disseminate early-warning information, revive indigenous ecological knowledge, and foster social cohesion during climate-related emergencies. When embedded within urban planning and disaster-risk frameworks, such interventions enhance trust, inclusivity, and last-mile communication—critical factors in informal settlements and high-density neighbourhoods where conventional planning tools often prove inadequate. Leveraged thoughtfully, art and design move beyond aesthetics to become low-cost, scalable instruments of public health, climate literacy, and urban resilience.
In India, such approaches can directly complement existing policy instruments and urban realities. Under Heat Action Plans (HAPs) adopted by cities like Ahmedabad, Nagpur, and Bhubaneswar, art-led community engagement can support education and communication, which is particularly important given the country’s linguistic diversity. The use of colour-coded murals, shaded public installations, and locally intelligible signages can convey heat-risk alerts, cooling behaviours, and access to water or shelters. Hand-drawn maps of contingency plans such as where to get clean water or backup power supplies are also useful.
In smaller Indian towns, where infrastructure deficits and linguistic diversity may limit the reach of official advisories, co-created visual tools and participatory design efforts can improve awareness of flood risks, sanitation-related health threats, and evacuation routes, while strengthening community resilience. In coastal cities such as Mumbai, Chennai, Kochi, and Visakhapatnam, public art and spatial design can help efficiently communicate concerns about sea-level rise, storm-surge risks, and the importance of mangrove or wetland conservation, while reinforcing resilience through culturally grounded narratives. Art and design ought to be embedded in grassroots urban planning to better translate national and municipal climate strategies into actionable, community-level resilience across India’s diverse urban landscapes.
Under the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) guidelines, participatory visual communication and community-designed public spaces can help strengthen disaster preparedness, early warning dissemination, and post-disaster recovery, particularly in high-risk urban wards. Within AMRUT (Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation), such approaches can support water security, heat mitigation, and green infrastructure goals through neighbourhood-scale design solutions and citizen science or other engagement around nature-based interventions.
The Smart Cities Mission needs to provide scope to integrate public art, tactical urbanism, and climate-responsive design as tools for inclusive resilience rather than purely technological optimisation which tends to fail under current climate conditions. In coastal cities, in alignment with the Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) framework, art and design can enhance public awareness of no-development zones, ecosystem buffers, and climate risks, while reinforcing community stewardship of mangroves, wetlands, and shoreline commons. Embedding these practices within formal programmes can bridge the gap between national policy intent and lived urban experience, ensuring that climate resilience is not only planned, but also socially understood and locally sustained in urban Indian settings.
As a multidisciplinary field, urban planning serves to both guide and direct the development and design of land, infrastructure, and services as places increasingly become urban. Planners utilise diverse disciplines for policy, including land use, transportation, housing, public spaces, and environmental considerations that benefit health.[23]
Urban planning in India remains a struggle due to rapid urbanisation, which tends to outpace infrastructure and ignore local contexts. Challenges, including fractured governance, often lead to unplanned and unregulated growth and sprawl, inefficient use of resources, and other social inequities. The scale of illegal and informal construction amplifies existing issues of traffic congestion and water scarcity as central plans often fail to consider or adapt to local needs. Seventy percent of urban development is unauthorised. Meanwhile, top-down approaches often bypass local governments or prioritise the national agenda over city-specific problems. The smart cities mission, for instance, in Kochi, reflected central government plans rather than local demands.[24] Limited public participation and rigid hierarchies prevent easy adaptability, while the views of vulnerable groups are often omitted in mainstream planning.
In practice, India’s urban planning remains extremely fragmented, reliant on outdated land-use zoning and short-term projects that tend to omit integrated, long-term visions of sustainability. There is a need for proactive, grassroots, and more holistic planning that incorporates climate resilience into masterplans. Heat Action Plans from Pune and Ahmedabad offer examples of linking economic development with health and climate strategies.[25] Integrated urban planning approaches that combine community engagement and emissions reduction can address interconnected issues such as waste management and heat stress.
A large share of urban India’s population lives in moderate to high seismic zones, where enforcement of building and safety codes remains weak. High-rise buildings often do not comply with standards. Rapid, often unplanned vertical growth in cities has led to an increased likelihood of damage vis-a-vis disasters like flash floods or earthquakes. However, the flaw of top-down urban planning is not just a misalignment of national designs and plans, but a lack of consideration for the smaller infrastructures that non-motorised transport and pedestrian users of the city experience: pavements, benches, and other common infrastructure have not been thoughtfully designed and are often made of heat-trapping materials such as metal and glass.
These plans tend to miss out on efficacy due to limited public input and misalignment with local needs: insufficient community engagement, high costs with low returns, and centralised priorities tend to impose standard, uniform decisions that are disconnected from on-ground realities. The use of materials, methods, and designs that are out of sync with ground conditions can create dead zones[a] that overlook access to food, nutritional, social and green space requirements for communities.
There are often few or no mechanisms for inclusive demographic involvement, and a shortage of urban planners (1 per 100,000 people), as well as fractured governance, further add to the challenges.[26] Regulatory frameworks tend to emphasise land-use zoning over climate resilience or inclusive growth, ignoring informal settlements and natural resources, for instance. Failing to address local needs often results in inefficient or misplaced implementation; there is also a general lack of accountability and coordination between national, state, and local priorities.
Disaster preparedness is a policy realm that offers the possibility of multi-stakeholder engagement for practical purposes. In the context of India’s climate change challenges, resilient urban planning should build upon people’s insights and knowledge about the places in which they live.[27] Disaster relief and resilience (DRR) plans based on grassroots urban planning should become a policy goal for Indian cities, as urban planning can be a useful tool for engaging communities and organising resources in case of emergency across space. Urban planning in the context of DRR can help democratise public spaces and enable conversations about preparedness through creative scenario building. This might facilitate the re-establishing of ties that have been eroded through the atomisation of people in the modern world. The current urban planning status quo begs the question of how better to involve communities and grassroots groups in climate and health action and planning processes.
In 2010, a heatwave in Ahmedabad caused over 1,300 deaths, forcing the city to develop a Heat Action Plan that included a tiered and colour-coded warning system which offered information about cooling shelters; how to access health workers; and even leveraging colorful murals to communicate to low-literacy communities. This resulted in a 25-percent reduction in heat-related mortality. The causal chain here would be: planning art-based interventions that are tiered warnings and leverage community infrastructure to reduce ambient exposure during heatwaves, thus reducing mortality and allowing for institutional capacity to be scaled in other cities. In DRR, the most effective responses are self-organised and spontaneous rather than those led by governments, NGOs, or private actors. Researchers like Greenfield,[28] Acciavati,[29] and Wahl[30] offer compendiums of unique approaches to not just grassroots organising, but also of citizen science that serves as an independent form of monitoring and accountability.
A 2015 study of flood response in Chennai demonstrated how self-organised community networks offered the fastest and most effective relief in place of overwhelmed state responses. Informal settlement mapping helped direct relief to the most vulnerable, and art-based education helped raise awareness about waterborne disease risks. The lesson here is that communities with prior participatory mapping experience were substantially more prepared and resilient. Chennai’s post-flood management relied on community networks and integrating art for awareness-raising.[31]
DRR relies upon decentralised networks that are effectively able to leverage first responders. Training and equipping ASHA (Accredited Social Health Activist) workers, for instance, builds a frontline of health responses during a climate emergency, and making communities aware of them can help to preposition field hospitals and even medical supply chains as necessary. Focusing on urban planning interventions for climate resilience helps guide financing mechanisms for post-disaster recovery.
The following recommendations cover key actions, government responsibility, and potential financial and measurable indicators of progress. Integrated urban planning approaches that combine communication, engagement, and emissions reduction can address interrelated issues such as waste management and heat stress.
Funds, volunteers, and other resources must be allocated to research and address the climate change-air pollution-public health nexus as a priority. Indian cities require independent ground monitoring mechanisms to observe changing disease burdens and transmission patterns, as well as to assess related health impacts. This requires appropriate local agency to respond to the various needs that might arise. Within budgets, funds must also be allocated for post-disaster recovery and relief planning by supporting existing networks and organisations—this leverages grassroots insights and knowledge.
Urban planning and design may be used to delineate and preserve green spaces in cities, particularly forests as critical infrastructure and protect them from exploitation. Financial support for traditional and vernacular forms of architecture which are more resilient is an important area of regulation and financing. Planning smaller design interventions or infrastructures for people, like shaded pavements and tree-lined parks, can offer passive cooling through shade and sprinklers.
Urban spaces are to be planned for people, and not cars, through land-use planning: planning of low-emission zones (LEZs); conserving carbon-trapping forest areas; and designing green spaces that encourage shade through tree cover. It would also include an adequate number of clinics and hospitals, training networks of first responders and ASHA workers, and designing the outreach for health-related messaging.
Regulating emissions for vehicles and industries through pollution controls and buy-back schemes could be useful in creating a shift towards greener and cleaner energy economies across sectors. This could be based on financial incentives for public transport or e-vehicle use, as well as disincentives and similar financial mechanisms to dissuade private vehicles from parts of the city at specific hours. Transport modes can also be accessibility-based: for instance, younger people should be encouraged to use public transport to increase active living, while the elderly or persons with disabilities should be given priority for private vehicle use. Free bus or metro passes for women and children, as well as train and bus tickets, can incentivise a shift towards greener, mass public transport modes. Car-free zones can be created for safer play and its interrelated benefits.
Research has demonstrated that urban cooling may be guided by nature to reduce the UHI effect exacerbated by construction and urbanisation. Nature-based solutions (NbS) offer cooling effects that can be achieved at the intersection of green and blue solutions.[b] Tree canopies offer shade and also allow for evaporation, which can reduce peak summer temperatures. Water bodies are heat sinks, while wind channels can help disperse hot air, and lighter colours will reflect more heat. Naturally porous materials like slate can promote evapotranspiration. NbS can therefore lower urban temperatures by offering shade and promoting evapotranspiration, while acting as heat sinks. It is also important to encourage the conservation of forests—not just for the benefits of tree cover, but for the role that old trees play as carbon traps. Wild spaces are crucial within urban areas, and are often the result of concerted urban planning decisions.
Investing nationally and locally in cleaner energy sources for buildings and transport, while supporting a shift in available technologies in the economy, is crucial. Framing this as being beneficial for healthier urban planning could also incorporate designing child-friendly, safe streets that allow for active living. This is dire, since road accidents cause an estimated 1.19 million deaths annually. Meanwhile, trapped pollutants from increasingly heavy traffic and unregulated pollution from industries including construction, are harmful to pedestrian commuters as well as nearby communities. Accountability and coordination, as well as fiscal allocation amongst assorted actors living in urban and rural spaces, is key to developing effective resilience building plans, which promote the well-being of communities.
Urban planning priorities ought to support grassroots, self-organised groups, citizen scientists, and other specialists/researchers whose findings may be relevant but beyond the scope of government work. This includes NGOs and other civil society networks. All sectors and stakeholders must become involved in preparing for disaster relief and responses, which will require assorted forms of creativity to be inclusive. Research collated in the work of Greenfield,[32] among others,[33] has shown that self-organised networks can respond almost two times faster and more effectively in cases of disaster and in the provision of relief. Facilitating people-led town-halls or community-based discussions can leverage knowledge and observations to fill in the theoretical frameworks that tend to guide policymakers. Inviting ideas from the public through creative modes is also an effective way for public policy to engage people in necessary policy processes, and to instil a sense of civic responsibility among people.
The community-based mapping of and with vulnerable populations like the poor, children, and the elderly can ensure their rights while revealing sensible future designs for passive cooling, among others; it is a creative way of informal needs assessment and resource allocation related to climate and health. Arshi Mehboob noted in June 2022 that, “a severe heatwave struck Delhi’s urban slums, with temperatures exceeding 45°C for days. The heat led to dehydration, heatstroke, and exacerbated respiratory issues, especially among pregnant women, children, and elderly residents.”[34] Much of this could be quickly addressed with appropriate resource and network visualisations to respond quickly and effectively.
Creative exercises can help communicate climate change and inform city- and sub-city-level climate and heat action plans, which account for site-specific climate and health issues, and can help better direct government-led air pollution abatement policies.[35] Community mapping is a way to creatively reimagine spaces for cars as places for people: play streets and shaded green spaces encourage social interaction, movement and activity, which are crucial for well-being, but are often compromised due to unregulated, infrastructure-related emissions. Nodal residents can be trained and prepared to lead communities when disasters will inevitably hit, leveraging the expert insights as nodes in a network of first responders.
Although India is by far not the largest per capita carbon emitter, its cities absorb the disproportionate health consequences of climate change. Those who experience the highest exposure to the negative health impacts of climate change are also largely absent from planning processes. Involving vulnerable and minority populations in policy processes—for their observations and leveraging these insights for their protection—is not just an urban planning exercise but is crucial for future resilience and effective disaster recovery.
Furthermore, in the interest of biodiversity conservation, urban planners must consider the needs of all forms of non-human life as part of a balanced ecosystems approach. The Global South is home to more than 15 percent of the world's flora and 12 percent of the fauna. These regions are simultaneously experiencing some of the most disproportionate biodiversity decline and climate change vulnerabilities, globally.[36] By resisting the urge to homogenise and paying attention to varied socioeconomic and political contexts, policymakers—with the help of assorted specialists—can more effectively prepare for a resilient future.
The four pillars outlined in this brief can offer policymakers pragmatic pathways to connect health impact assessments with disaster responses via targeted grassroots preparedness. To build upon a statement by Maria Neira, WHO Director, Department of Environment, Climate Change and Health: “If the purpose of urban planning is not for human health, then what is it for?”[37] Perhaps, the purpose is to direct the well-being of a balanced ecosystem, with consideration for all people and non-human life forms.
Shriya Malhotra is an artist and researcher. She studied International Affairs, with a focus on cities and urbanisation, from The New School.

They are typically caused by rigid zoning, car-centric infrastructure (like parking lots), and blank architectural walls. These spaces disrupt city connectivity and feel unsafe.
